**Triage (Issue 1):** `0.30000000000000004 !== 0.3` from `assert.equal` — not a self-describing config gap, not a runtime-internal opaque stack trace. Names a failure type (numeric mismatch) without naming the cause → **Class B**. Single file given inline, already read.

## Root Cause
IEEE-754 double-precision floats can't exactly represent decimal fractions like `0.1` and `0.2`, so `0.1 + 0.2` evaluates to the nearest representable double, `0.30000000000000004`, not the mathematical `0.3` — a limitation that integer-cent arithmetic was previously masking by never summing fractional binary values.

## Evidence
- The function as given: `total = items => items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)` — a plain float accumulator, no rounding anywhere in the chain.
- `0.1` in binary64 is `0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625`, and `0.2` is `0.200000000000000011102230246251565404236316680908203125`. Their sum rounds to the nearest double, which prints as `0.30000000000000004`. This is deterministic IEEE-754 behavior, not an environment or Node-version quirk.
- Stated change: totals moved from integer cents → float dollars. Integer cents (`10 + 20 = 30`) are exact in binary; float dollars (`0.1 + 0.2`) are not. The migration is what exposed the bug — it was always latent in floating point, just never triggered when values were integers.

## Call Chain
`total([0.1, 0.2])` → `reduce` accumulates float sum → result is the IEEE-754 nearest-double artifact → `assert.equal(result, 0.3)` fails because `0.3`'s own nearest-double representation differs from the accumulated sum's nearest-double representation.

## Fix
Round the result to cent precision after summation, since money has no meaningful sub-cent value:

```js
export const total = items => Math.round(items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) * 100) / 100
```

This does not re-architect the money representation — it's the minimal patch that makes float-dollar summation produce cent-accurate results.

## Verification
Run `node --test test/invoice.test.js` and confirm `assert.equal(total([0.1, 0.2]), 0.3)` passes. Also check adjacent precision-sensitive cases don't regress, e.g. `total([0.1, 0.1, 0.1])` should equal `0.3`, and a non-trivial case like `total([19.99, 5.01])` should equal `25`.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED. Adversarial probe — alternative explanations considered and eliminated:
- *Summation order/associativity bug in `reduce`*: ruled out — with only two addends, order is irrelevant; the imprecision is inherent to the binary representation of the operands themselves, not the fold direction.
- *Test using the wrong assertion (`assert.equal` instead of an epsilon-based comparison)*: this is a real secondary issue but not the root cause of *why the sum is wrong* — even a correct epsilon comparison wouldn't explain away the fact that money stored as raw floats will keep drifting; rounding at the money boundary is the right fix either way.
No alternative survives as the explanation for the literal printed value `0.30000000000000004`.

## Handoffs
→ ndv-build (implementation) · `total()` (inline snippet, invoice module): confirmed root cause is unrounded float summation after the integer-cents→float-dollars migration; apply `Math.round(sum * 100) / 100` after the reduce; verify with `node --test test/invoice.test.js` passing `assert.equal(total([0.1, 0.2]), 0.3)`.
→ ndv-architect (structure) · invoice totals module: storing/summing currency as raw floats (post integer-cents→float-dollars migration) is structurally fragile — every future sum/subtract risks the same class of precision drift; worth evaluating integer-cents or a decimal type as the canonical representation rather than rounding at each call site.

## Root Cause

The handler resolves each member's avatar with a **separate sequential DB round-trip inside a `for`/`await` loop** (classic N+1 query pattern), so total request latency scales linearly with team size — at 4,000 members this serializes 4,001 round-trips in a single request, which exceeds the 30s timeout; small teams stay under threshold only because N is small, not because anything else differs.

## Evidence

- Code: `members = await db.query(...)` returns the full team, then `for (const m of members) { m.avatar = await db.query(...) }` — each iteration blocks on its own round-trip before the next starts. No `Promise.all`, no batching, no join.
- "Changed recently: avatars added last week" lines up exactly with this loop's introduction — there is no other diff candidate in the handler.
- Scaling signature matches the symptom precisely: small teams (few members) → few sequential awaits → <1s; Platform (4,000 members) → 4,000 sequential awaits → timeout. If the slowness were in the initial `SELECT * FROM members` alone, team size wouldn't matter this sharply at the per-member granularity described — it's the *per-member* loop, not the bulk select, that scales with N.

**Adversarial probe:** could this instead be an unindexed `avatars.member_id` making each individual lookup slow, rather than the serial-loop structure itself? Even if indexed and each avatar query took 1ms server-side, 4,000 sequential (not parallel) round-trips at typical network/driver RTT (several ms each) already sums into seconds-to-tens-of-seconds territory, and the code offers no concurrency to amortize that regardless of per-query speed. A missing index would make it worse, not cause it — removing the serial-await structure is necessary either way. No alternative explanation accounts for the sharp small-team-vs-large-team divergence as cleanly as the N+1 loop does. No surviving alternative.

## Call Chain

`GET /teams/42/members` → bulk member fetch (fast) → loop over 4,000 members → 4,000 sequential `await db.query(... avatars ...)` calls, each waiting on the prior → cumulative latency exceeds 30s → request times out.

## Fix

Out of scope for root-cause confirmation — this is a performance bottleneck (N+1 query pattern), not a correctness bug, so I'm identifying and handing it off rather than writing the fix. The shape of the needed fix (for whoever picks this up): replace the per-member avatar loop with a single batched query (`WHERE member_id = ANY($1)` / a join) keyed on all member IDs from the first query, then map avatars back onto members in memory — eliminating the N+1 round-trips entirely.

## Verification

Once the fix lands: `GET /teams/42/members` should return in well under 1s (matching small-team latency), and the avatar lookup should execute as exactly one additional query regardless of team size — confirm by logging/counting queries per request (should go from N+1 to 2) and re-testing against the 4,000-member Platform team specifically, not just a small team.

## Verdict

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — the serial N+1 avatar-fetch loop is the cause, not a side effect of something else; evidence is the loop structure itself plus the team-size-proportional symptom divergence, and the adversarial probe found no alternative explanation that survives (an unindexed avatars table would compound but not cause this).

## Handoffs

→ ndv-optimize (performance) · the avatar-fetch loop in the `/teams/:id/members` handler: sequential per-member `await db.query` calls form an N+1 pattern; needs replacing with a single batched query (`ANY($1)`/join) over all member IDs from the initial result, with results mapped back in memory.

## Root Cause
The loop's bound was changed from `i < xs.length` to `i <= xs.length`, so it reads one index past the array's end on every call, and `sum += undefined` poisons the total to `NaN`.

## Evidence
Traced `avg([1, 2, 3])` by hand against the inline source:
- `xs.length` = 3, valid indices are 0, 1, 2.
- Loop condition `i <= xs.length` lets `i` reach 3.
- `i=0`: `sum = 0 + 1 = 1`
- `i=1`: `sum = 1 + 2 = 3`
- `i=2`: `sum = 3 + 3 = 6`
- `i=3`: `xs[3]` is `undefined` (out of bounds) → `sum = 6 + undefined = NaN`
- `return NaN / 3` → `NaN`, matching the reported actual value exactly.

**Adversarial probe:** checked for an alternative explanation — e.g. `xs.length === 0` would also produce `NaN` via `0/0`, but the failing call uses `[1, 2, 3]` (length 3), so the zero-length path is not in play here and doesn't account for the observed failure. No other candidate cause fits both the symptom and the "loop was simplified last week" change note.

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — off-by-one is the sole cause for this reproduction; no competing hypothesis survives the probe.

## Call Chain
`test/avg.test.js` calls `avg([1,2,3])` → loop over-reads → `sum` becomes `NaN` → `NaN / xs.length` → assertion compares `NaN` to `2` → fails.

## Fix
```js
for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++) sum += xs[i]
```
Change `<=` to `<`. Nothing else in the function needs to change for this symptom.

## Verification
Run `node --test test/avg.test.js` — `assert.equal(avg([1, 2, 3]), 2)` should pass. Spot-check the trace: `i` now runs 0,1,2 only; `sum` ends at 6; `6/3 = 2`.

## Root Cause
The report computes "today" from `now.toISOString()` — the UTC calendar date — not the viewer's local calendar date, so any order placed in local evening hours that crosses into the next UTC day gets filed under the wrong business day; Redis is not involved.

## Evidence
Read the function as given (Class B — ambiguous symptom, single function, no file traversal needed):

```js
function ordersToday(orders, now = new Date()) {
  const today = now.toISOString().slice(0, 10)
  return orders.filter(o => o.createdAt.toISOString().slice(0, 10) === today)
}
```

Both `today` and each `o.createdAt` are reduced to `.toISOString().slice(0,10)` — a **UTC** date string. Walking the repro exactly as stated:

- User timezone America/New_York, standard offset UTC-5. Order placed 21:00 local on day D → stored `createdAt` = day D, 02:00 UTC on **day D+1** (21:00 + 5h crosses UTC midnight).
- Next morning, local time, the viewer opens the report. `now` at that point also falls on UTC day D+1.
- `today` (UTC D+1) === `createdAt`'s UTC date (D+1) → the order matches and is included in "today's" (D+1) report.
- From the viewer's local perspective, that order was placed D, "yesterday evening" — yet it shows in D+1's report.

This reproduces the exact symptom — "yesterday's late-evening orders" leaking into today's report — and it reproduces **only** for offsets where local evening pushes past UTC midnight (UTC-5 and similar; UTC-0 users would never see this, since their local day and UTC day never diverge). That matches "only for users in UTC-5" precisely.

Adversarial probe against the Redis hypothesis: a cache-staleness bug would be intermittent/time-decaying — flushing it would fix the report until the cache repopulates, and the error would not correlate with a specific timezone offset or a specific local hour band. Here the bug is **deterministic and purely a function of offset and clock hour** — it reproduces every single night for every UTC-5 (or further-behind) user whose order lands in that evening window, cache or no cache. The "cache config hasn't changed in a year" fact, paired with "the report query was rewritten last sprint," points at the rewrite, not the cache — that's the actual delta. No alternative cause survives the check: **CONFIRMED**.

## Call Chain
Order placed (local 21:00) → stored with UTC `createdAt` one calendar day ahead of local → `ordersToday` buckets by UTC date instead of viewer's local date → misfiled order surfaces in the wrong day's report on the morning read.

## Fix
Bucket by the viewer's local calendar day, not UTC. Minimal shape (actual timezone source — session/user profile — is for the implementer to wire in):

```js
function ordersToday(orders, now = new Date(), timeZone) {
  const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-CA', { timeZone, year: 'numeric', month: '2-digit', day: '2-digit' })
  const today = fmt.format(now)
  return orders.filter(o => fmt.format(o.createdAt) === today)
}
```

`timeZone` must be the viewer's IANA zone (e.g. `America/New_York`), not left to default to UTC — that default would silently reintroduce the same bug.

## Verification
1. Unit test: order `createdAt` = `2026-11-07T02:00:00Z` (21:00 EST on 2026-11-06), `now` = `2026-11-07T14:00:00Z`, `timeZone` = `America/New_York` → assert the order is **excluded** from `ordersToday` (it belongs to 2026-11-06 locally).
2. Re-run the original repro: place an order at 21:00 America/New_York, open the report the next local morning — confirm it no longer appears.
3. Confirm no regression for UTC viewers (`timeZone: 'UTC'` should reproduce the original behavior exactly).

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED. Evidence: traced the exact repro arithmetic (offset + clock hour) against the UTC-slicing code and showed it reproduces the symptom deterministically and only for offsets where local evening crosses UTC midnight; ran the adversarial probe against the stated Redis-cache hypothesis and it fails — cache staleness can't explain a bug that is 100% reproducible, offset-dependent, and correlated with last sprint's query rewrite rather than an untouched cache config. Flushing Redis will not fix this; the bug will recur the same night for the same users regardless.

## Handoffs
→ ndv-build (implementation) · `ordersToday` function: apply the local-timezone bucketing fix above, wiring `timeZone` from the viewer's profile/session instead of defaulting to UTC; verify with the unit test in Verification.
→ ndv-tester (coverage) · `ordersToday`: no test caught a timezone-boundary case across the rewrite last sprint — add cases for UTC-5/UTC-8/UTC+ offsets at the evening boundary hours.

## Root Cause
Dollar amounts are summed directly as IEEE‑754 double-precision floats, and most decimal fractions (0.1, 0.2, 0.3 among them) have no exact binary representation — so `0.1 + 0.2` doesn't land on 0.3, it lands on the nearest representable double, 0.30000000000000004.

## Evidence
- The function given is `total = items => items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)` — plain float addition, no rounding or cent-scaling anywhere in the chain.
- The reported failure value, `0.30000000000000004`, is the textbook binary64 result of `0.1 + 0.2` — not a reduce bug, not an order-of-operations bug, just the known non-exact encoding of those two literals.
- The brief states the regression's proximate cause directly: totals were moved from integer cents (exact under addition) to float dollars (inexact under addition). That migration is what removed the exactness guarantee — before it, `10 + 20` (cents) was exact; now `0.1 + 0.2` (dollars) is not.

## Call Chain
`total([0.1, 0.2])` → `reduce` adds the two doubles → result is the nearest representable double to 0.30000000000000004440892... → `assert.equal` compares it bit-for-bit against the double nearest to 0.3 → mismatch.

## Fix
Scale to integer cents inside the reduce, then convert back once at the end, so the summation itself is exact integer arithmetic instead of accumulating binary float error:

```js
export const total = items =>
  items.reduce((s, x) => s + Math.round(x * 100), 0) / 100
```

Rounding *before* summing (not only at the end) matters for invoices with many line items — rounding only the final sum lets per-item float error accumulate past half a cent before it's corrected; rounding each item to its nearest cent first means the summation itself is exact integers, with no accumulation possible.

## Verification
Run `node --test test/invoice.test.js`. `assert.equal(total([0.1, 0.2]), 0.3)` should now pass — `10 + 20 = 30` (exact integers), `30 / 100` produces the same double as the literal `0.3`. Also worth checking a multi-item case like `total([0.1, 0.1, 0.1])` against `0.3` to confirm no accumulation drift survives.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED. Adversarial probe: the alternative explanation — "the test assertion is just too strict, use an epsilon comparison instead" — doesn't survive, because it only hides the symptom in this one test. The underlying computation would still produce invoice totals that are fractions of a cent off from the true decimal sum, which is the thing that actually matters for money, not just this assertion. The float-dollar summation is the cause, not the test's strictness.

## Root Cause

The handler builds the SQL statement by raw string concatenation of unescaped user input (`req.query.name`); any value containing a single quote terminates the string literal early, leaving a stray unquoted token that Postgres can't parse — this is a SQL injection flaw (CWE-89), and the "syntax error" is just its most visible symptom.

## Evidence

Single line of the route is the entire query path:

```js
const rows = await db.query("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name = '" + req.query.name + "'")
```

For `req.query.name = "O'Brien"`, the interpolated statement becomes:

```sql
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name = 'O'Brien'
```

Postgres closes the string literal at the second `'` (after the `O`), parses `'O'` as a complete literal, then hits the bare identifier `Brien` where it expects an operator or end of clause — hence `syntax error at or near "Brien"`. Every other name works only because no other common test name happens to contain a quote; the bug has nothing to do with "O'Brien" specifically and nothing to do with anything changed recently — it's been live since this concatenation pattern was written, consistent with "nothing changed in this file for months."

## Call Chain

`req.query.name` ("O'Brien") → concatenated unescaped into the SQL text → `db.query()` sends malformed SQL to Postgres → Postgres parser rejects the stray token → driver throws → no try/catch in the handler → Express's default error handler returns HTTP 500 (and, depending on Express/NODE_ENV config, may echo the raw Postgres error message back to the caller — see Warning finding below).

## Fix

Not written here — root cause is a security vulnerability, so per the debugging domain's scope boundary this goes to `ndv-secure`, not patched in place. (The eventual fix is a parameterized query, e.g. `db.query("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name = $1", [req.query.name])` — named here only so the handoff is actionable, not as a patch I'm applying.)

## Verification

Once a parameterized-query fix is applied: `GET /customers?name=O'Brien` should return normal JSON (matching row or empty array) with HTTP 200, not 500. As a regression/security check, also try payloads like `?name=' OR '1'='1` and `?name='; DROP TABLE customers; --` and confirm they are treated as literal name values (no extra rows returned, no schema effect) rather than altering query logic.

## Verdict

**CONFIRMED.** Adversarial probe: considered alternatives — client-side URL-encoding mangling the apostrophe (ruled out; Express's query parser decodes it to a literal `'` before it reaches the handler, and the error text contains the literal name fragment, proving it arrived intact); a DB-side trigger/constraint on `customers` (ruled out; the error is a parser-stage syntax error, which occurs before any trigger/constraint logic runs); a recent regression (ruled out; brief states no change in this file for months, and the concatenation pattern shown is unconditionally broken for any quote-containing input, so it would have failed this way since it was first written). No alternative explanation survives — the string-concatenation construction is sufficient and necessary to produce this exact symptom.

## Handoffs

→ **ndv-secure (vulnerability)** · route handler, `app.get('/customers', ...)`: SQL injection via unescaped string concatenation of `req.query.name` into the query text. Exploit vector: any request can inject arbitrary SQL fragments into the `WHERE` clause — e.g. `?name=' OR '1'='1` returns the entire `customers` table, and depending on the `pg` driver's multi-statement handling, stacked queries (`?name='; DROP TABLE customers; --`) or UNION-based payloads could read or damage data outside the intended scope. Needs a parameterized query, not string building.

→ **ndv-tester (coverage)** · same handler: no test exercises names containing quotes, SQL metacharacters, or injection payloads — this exact bug class ships silently without one.

→ **ndv-telemetry (observability)** · same handler: the `db.query` call has no try/catch and no logging, so malformed-query failures surface only as a generic 500 to the caller with nothing captured server-side — the only reason this reached a human was a user noticing the broken search, not monitoring.

**Assumption I'm flagging, not guessing past:** I'm not shown a `beforeEach`/`afterEach` reset for `db` in this file. 1. **Isolate state per test** — give each test a fresh store instead of sharing the singleton (e.g. a `beforeEach` that resets/recreates `db`'s underlying data, or a factory that returns a new instance per test). ## Root Cause
`setCount(count + 1)` inside the `setInterval` callback closes over the `count` value from the render that created the effect (0, forever) — because the effect's dependency array is `[]`, that callback is created exactly once and never sees a fresh `count`, so every tick computes `0 + 1` and calls `setCount(1)` again and again.

## Evidence
- `useEffect(..., [])` → runs once on mount, never re-created, never re-reads a fresh closure.
- The interval itself is healthy (console.log fires every second, per the brief) — so the failure is in what the callback *computes*, not in whether it runs. That rules out a timer/cleanup bug.
- `setCount(count + 1)` uses the captured identifier `count` directly rather than the functional updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` — the textbook signature of this exact closure bug in a hooks migration.
- React bails out of re-rendering once `setCount(1)` is called with the same value repeatedly (1 === 1), which is why the UI freezes at 1 rather than cycling through 0 → 1 → 0 → 1.

## Call Chain
Mount → effect runs once → interval callback closure fixes `count` at 0 → every tick: `setCount(0 + 1)` → state becomes 1 on the first tick and is reasserted as 1 on every subsequent tick → render shows `1` forever despite the timer firing correctly.

## Fix
```jsx
const id = setInterval(() => setCount(c => c + 1), 1000)
```
Replace the direct `count` reference with the functional updater. No dependency-array change needed — this is the correct fix precisely because it avoids re-creating the interval on every tick.

## Verification
Open `/dashboard`, watch the counter for 5 seconds: expect `0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5…` instead of freezing at `1`. Equivalent automated check: render `Ticker` under `jest.useFakeTimers()`, advance 5000ms, assert the displayed count is `5`.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED. Adversarial probe — checked for alternative explanations before accepting this one:
- Effect re-running and leaking multiple intervals? No — deps `[]` means it runs once; cleanup only fires on unmount. Ruled out.
- Re-render suppressed by memoization or a stale key? None present in this snippet. Ruled out.
- Interval silently dying? No — console.log firing every second (per repro) confirms the timer itself is fine. Ruled out.
No alternative survives the symptom; the stale-closure read is the only one that explains both "log fires every second" and "value frozen at 1" simultaneously.

## Handoffs (if any)
None — this is a self-contained closure bug, not a security, performance, architectural, or coverage gap. The fix is a one-line change Pierce/Acute hand to the human directly, since no build-execution agent was named in the brief:

→ ndv-build (implementation) · `Ticker` component, `useEffect` callback: confirmed root cause above; fix is replacing `setCount(count + 1)` with `setCount(c => c + 1)`; verify via the 5-second observation or fake-timer test above.

If that lint rule isn't active in this project, it's worth turning on — it would have caught this before the hooks migration shipped. Suggestion-severity, no action taken.

## Root Cause
`loadConfig` requires `QUEUE_URL` from `process.env`, but the local `.env` file was never updated to match the provider migration that renamed/introduced this key in `.env.example` — so the variable is unset at startup.

## Evidence
- The error is self-describing (Error Triage **Class A** — config gap): it names the missing variable directly, `QUEUE_URL`, with no ambiguity about type, value, or logic path.
- Stack trace confirms this fires at the first validation gate, `config.js:14` inside `loadConfig`, called immediately from `main` (`worker.js:3`) — before any queue connection logic runs. Nothing downstream is implicated.
- Brief states the proximate change: queue moved to a new provider and `.env.example` was updated. That is the exact shape of a Class A gap — the template moved, the local `.env` didn't follow.
- Adversarial probe — alternative causes checked and ruled out by the evidence available: (a) dotenv not loading at all would blank *every* env var, not just one named in the error, so that's not it; (b) a code-side typo (config.js reading a different key than `.env.example` now defines) can't be distinguished from "simply unset" without reading `.env.example`'s new key name and `config.js:14` — flagging this as the one gap the Class A shortcut leaves open.

## Call Chain
`main` (`src/worker.js:3`) → `loadConfig` (`src/config.js:14`) → validation check on `process.env.QUEUE_URL` fails because the key is absent from the loaded environment.

## Fix
Not a source change — a config action: add `QUEUE_URL=<new provider's queue URL>` to the local `.env` file, using the exact key name now present in `.env.example` (confirm it is still literally `QUEUE_URL` and not renamed to something like `QUEUE_ENDPOINT` or `BROKER_URL` during the provider swap — that distinction decides whether this is the whole fix or whether `config.js:14` also needs its expected key name updated).

## Verification
Run `npm run worker` again after setting the variable. Success is the worker starting without the `Missing required environment variable` error and proceeding to its next startup step (e.g., queue connection log/handshake).

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED for the "unset local `.env`" cause as the proximate trigger — the error message alone is sufficient per Class A triage, and the recent provider/`.env.example` change independently corroborates it. **UNCONFIRMED** on one narrow sub-point: whether `.env.example`'s new key is still named `QUEUE_URL` (pure config gap) or was renamed to something else and `config.js:14` is reading a stale key name (config gap *plus* a one-line code change). Diffing `.env.example` against `config.js:14`'s expected key closes this gap — that single comparison is what the Class A shortcut deliberately skipped.

## Handoffs (if any)
None required for the fix itself. One observation worth carrying forward, not a formal handoff: if the provider migration renamed or added other queue-related keys beyond `QUEUE_URL`, each will surface as the same one-at-a-time crash on next startup — worth a single pass reconciling `.env` against the full `.env.example` now, rather than fixing this one variable and hitting the next crash immediately after.

## Root Cause
The handler awaits one `avatars` query per member **sequentially inside a `for` loop** instead of batching or parallelizing, so total latency scales linearly with team size — 4,000 members means 4,000 serial round-trips, which is what pushes the Platform team past the 30s timeout while small teams (few iterations) stay fast.

## Evidence
Read directly from the attached handler — no grep needed, the whole route is in scope:
```js
for (const m of members) {
  m.avatar = await db.query('SELECT url FROM avatars WHERE member_id = $1', [m.id])
}
```
`await` inside the loop body blocks the next iteration from starting until the current query resolves — this is the classic N+1 pattern. "Changed recently: avatars added last week" lines up exactly with when this loop was introduced; before that, the handler would have been a single query.

**Adversarial probe (for CONFIRMED status):** could the bottleneck instead be the initial `SELECT * FROM members` on 4,000 rows, or DB pool exhaustion? Ruled out — a single indexed lookup by `team_id` over 4,000 rows wouldn't by itself blow a 30s budget, and pool exhaustion would show up as intermittent slowness across team sizes, not a response time that scales cleanly with member count the way described. The symptom's proportionality to member count points at the loop, not the first query or the pool. No alternative cause survives the probe.

## Call Chain
`GET /teams/42/members` → 1 fast query for members → loop fires 1 avatar query per member, **serially** → total time ≈ N × (per-query round-trip) → for N=4,000 this exceeds 30s; for small N it doesn't.

## Fix
Out of scope for this handoff — see classification below. Not writing a patch.

## Verification
Once remediated: load-test `GET /teams/42/members` (or any team with ~4,000+ synthetic members) and confirm (a) response completes well under the timeout, (b) query count issued to `avatars` is O(1) (one batched query) rather than O(n), and (c) each member's `avatar` field still maps to the correct member — a batch rewrite is an easy place to silently mismatch avatar-to-member pairing.

## Verdict
**CONFIRMED** — the N+1 sequential-await loop is the cause, not the symptom; the proportional scaling with member count and the timing of the avatar feature are both evidence, and the adversarial probe found no surviving alternative explanation.

---

## Also Noticed (total-perception sweep — not filtered out as "too small")

Acute's rule: everything that registers gets reported, classified after the fact. These were in frame while reading the same 6 lines; none are the confirmed root cause above, so none get a Fix, but none get dropped either.

- **Critical** — Neither `db.query` call has error handling. In this async Express handler, a rejected query has no `try/catch` and no `.catch`/`next(err)` — depending on Express version this can hang the request or crash the process on an unhandled rejection, which would *also* present as a timeout and could be masking or compounding the symptom above.
- **Critical** — No pagination/limit on the response. Even after fixing the N+1 pattern, this endpoint still serializes and returns up to 4,000+ full member objects (plus avatar URLs) in one JSON payload. Batching the avatar query fixes the *query count* problem, not the *unbounded response size* problem — the next large team will reveal this.
- **Warning** — `SELECT *` on `members` pulls every column indiscriminately. Inflates payload size and widens the field's exposure surface if the schema has columns not meant for this endpoint (unverified here — flagging, not asserting).
- **Warning** — No confirmation that `avatars.member_id` is indexed. If it isn't, each of the (soon-to-be-batched) avatar lookups could still be doing a scan, which would show up again as team size grows.
- **Suggestion** — Avatar URLs are a natural caching candidate (low churn, read-heavy) — worth a cache layer once the query shape is fixed.

## Handoffs
→ ndv-optimize (performance) · route handler, the `for...await` loop over `avatars`: N+1 sequential query pattern — replace with a single batched lookup (`WHERE member_id = ANY($1)` / `IN (...)`) or parallelize with `Promise.all`; this is the confirmed root cause of the timeout.
→ ndv-architect (structure) · same endpoint: no pagination/cursor on `/teams/:id/members` — response size is unbounded and will keep growing with team size even after the query fix.
→ ndv-tester (coverage) · same endpoint: no test exercises a large team (e.g., 1,000+ members); add a regression/load test asserting response time and query count stay bounded as team size grows, to catch any reintroduced N+1.

## Root Cause
`total` sums dollar amounts with native float addition (`s + x`), and binary floating point cannot represent decimal fractions like `0.1`/`0.2` exactly, so the sum accumulates representation error instead of the integer-cents arithmetic it replaced.

## Evidence
- `total([0.1, 0.2])` → `0.1 + 0.2` in IEEE-754 double precision is `0.30000000000000004`, not `0.3` — this is the textbook binary-float decimal-representation gap, independent of this codebase.
- Stated recent change: totals moved from **integer cents** (exact, since cents are integers) to **float dollars** (inexact, since most cent-valued dollar amounts have no exact binary representation). The migration itself removed the property that made the old arithmetic exact.
- `reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)` has no rounding step anywhere in the chain — nothing absorbs the per-addition drift before it's returned/compared.

## Call Chain
`assert.equal(total([0.1, 0.2]), 0.3)` → `total` reduces with raw `+` → returned value carries float drift → `assert.equal` (loose, coercion-based) still fails because `0.30000000000000004 !== 0.3` as numbers.

## Fix
Round the summed result to the cent (2 decimal places) before returning:

```js
export const total = items => Math.round(items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) * 100) / 100
```

This is the minimal patch that restores exact-cent output without reverting the dollars representation. It does not fix the underlying precision risk in multi-step chains (discounts, taxes, multi-currency) that touch `total`'s output before further math — see handoff below.

## Verification
Run `node --test test/invoice.test.js`. `assert.equal(total([0.1, 0.2]), 0.3)` should pass. Also spot-check a few more float-sensitive combinations (`[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` → `0.6`, `[1.005, 2.005]` → `3.01`) to confirm the rounding step, not luck, is what's passing.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED. Adversarial probe: considered whether the test itself is wrong (expecting an unreasonable exact value) — it isn't; `0.3` is the correct business total for `0.10 + 0.20`, so the defect is in `total`, not the assertion. Considered whether `assert.equal`'s coercion masks a different bug — it doesn't; both operands are numbers, no coercion is in play. No alternative root cause survives the probe.

- **Warning:** Using floats for any currency math at all is the structural choice that makes this class of bug recurring, not just this one call site. The rounding fix above patches the symptom at this function's boundary; any caller that adds/multiplies `total`'s *unrounded* intermediate values before this returns (if that pattern exists elsewhere) will still drift.
- **Warning:** No input validation in `total` — `items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)` will silently produce `NaN` or string-concatenate if a non-numeric line item slips in (e.g. `undefined`, a string price), and nothing here would surface that as an invoice-specific error.

## Reframing before the fix

Running the Domain Soundness Check on this brief: it conflates symptom and cause. "It's the Redis cache" is a *theory about* the symptom, not the symptom itself — the observed fact is "report shows yesterday's late orders, only for UTC‑5 users." Per protocol, I proceeded with the investigation rather than accepting the stated cause.

**It is not the cache.** The code you attached has no Redis, no cache layer, no stale-read path in it at all — and the one piece of context that actually points at a cause (*"the report query was rewritten last sprint; the cache config has not changed in a year"*) rules the cache **out**: the delta is in the query, not the cache. A cache explanation also doesn't fit the shape of the symptom — a stale cache would misbehave for everyone or clear on TTL, not selectively for one UTC offset.

## Root Cause
`ordersToday` buckets both "today" and each order's day using `toISOString().slice(0,10)`, which always renders the date in **UTC**, not the user's local timezone — so any order placed near local midnight in a negative-UTC-offset timezone gets bucketed into the wrong calendar day relative to that user's local "today."

## Evidence
- `now.toISOString().slice(0,10)` and `o.createdAt.toISOString().slice(0,10)` — both calls convert to UTC before slicing the date; no timezone parameter exists anywhere in the function signature.
- Reproduction trace: a New York user (UTC‑5) places an order at 21:00 local on day D. In UTC that instant is 02:00 on day **D+1** (`21:00 − (−5h)` → UTC runs 5h ahead of EST). `createdAt.toISOString()` therefore reports date **D+1**.
- Next morning, the report runs with `now` = server UTC time, also date **D+1**. `today === orderDate` → **D+1 === D+1** → the filter matches, so an order the user considers "yesterday evening" is pulled into *today's* report.
- UTC-aligned or positive-offset users don't see this because their local evening doesn't cross a UTC date boundary in the same way — explains why only UTC‑5 (and other negative-offset zones) are affected.
- "Changed recently" check: the query/function was rewritten last sprint — this is the delta. Cache config, unchanged for a year, is not.

## Call Chain
`ordersToday(orders, now)` → `now`/`createdAt` both coerced to UTC date strings → comparison is timezone-blind → order misassigned to the wrong local day → wrong rows surface in the "orders today" report.

## Fix
Bucket by the business/user's local calendar date, not UTC:

```js
function ordersToday(orders, now = new Date(), timeZone = 'UTC') {
  const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-CA', { timeZone, year: 'numeric', month: '2-digit', day: '2-digit' })
  const today = fmt.format(now)
  return orders.filter(o => fmt.format(o.createdAt) === today)
}
```
`timeZone` should be threaded through from the actual report/business timezone (or per-user timezone, if "today" is meant per-viewer) rather than defaulted silently to UTC.

## Verification
- Unit test: `createdAt = 2026-11-07T02:00:00Z` (= 2026-11-06 21:00 America/New_York), `now = 2026-11-07T13:00:00Z`, `timeZone = 'America/New_York'`.
  - Before fix: order is **included** (UTC dates match, D+1 === D+1) — reproduces the bug.
  - After fix: order is **excluded** (local dates are 11-06 vs 11-07) — confirms the fix.
- In production: re-run the report for a UTC‑5 account immediately after a ~21:00-local order and confirm it no longer appears until the following day's report.

## Verdict
**CONFIRMED.** Adversarial probe: searched for a cache-shaped explanation (stale read, TTL skew, key collision) that would explain a *UTC-offset-selective* symptom — none fits, since nothing in the shown path reads from or writes to a cache, and a cache issue wouldn't be offset-dependent. The timezone-blind date bucketing fully explains the symptom and is the thing that actually changed last sprint.

- **Warning:** No guard if `o.createdAt` isn't a `Date` instance — `.toISOString()` will throw rather than fail gracefully on malformed input.
- **Suggestion:** `toISOString()`/`slice` recomputed per order per call; trivial at report scale, not worth a separate performance handoff, but worth noting if `orders` grows large.
- **Suggestion:** No code comment documents that date bucketing is intentionally UTC vs. local — the ambiguity is exactly what let this ship unnoticed.

## Critical

### `repo.save` not awaited — function reports success before (or regardless of) actual outcome — `diff:3`
**Problem:** `updateProfile` is declared `async` but calls `repo.save(profile)` without `await`. This violates the stated constraint ("async/await everywhere") and breaks the function on two independent axes:
1. If `repo.save` returns a Promise (near-certain for a method named `save` on a `repo` — almost nothing persists synchronously), the `try/catch` wrapped around it is inert for async failures. A promise *rejection* from `repo.save` is not thrown into this call stack; it surfaces as an unhandled rejection elsewhere (or silently, depending on runtime config), and the local `catch (e)` never runs for that failure path.
2. Even setting aside #1 — the function returns `{ ok: true }` unconditionally, on every path, whether `repo.save` succeeded, failed synchronously and was caught, or is still in flight. The caller has no way to learn that a save failed.

**Impact:** Callers receive `{ ok: true }` for profile updates that never happened or are still pending. Data the UI/caller believes is persisted may not be — classic silent data loss from the caller's perspective, plus a race condition where callers that assume completion (e.g. immediately re-reading the profile) can observe stale data.

**Fix:** `await repo.save(profile)` inside the `try`, and make the return value depend on whether the catch ran (e.g. return `{ ok: false }` or rethrow/propagate the error) rather than hardcoding `{ ok: true }`.

**Adversarial probe (re-examination of this finding):** Could `repo.save` be synchronous, making the missing `await` harmless? Possible, but irrelevant to the finding's core: even in that case, the `catch` block still swallows the error and the function still returns `{ ok: true }` unconditionally — the "false success reported on failure" half of this bug survives regardless of `repo.save`'s sync/async nature. The "unawaited promise / race condition" half depends on `repo.save` being async, which the "async/await everywhere" constraint and the name `repo.save` both make highly likely. I could not disconfirm the finding from the given diff; it stands.

## Root Cause
The loop condition `i <= xs.length` runs one iteration past the last valid index, so on the final pass `xs[i]` reads `xs[3]` (out of bounds) which is `undefined`; `sum += undefined` makes `sum` permanently `NaN`, and `NaN / xs.length` stays `NaN`.

## Evidence
Traced the loop by hand for `xs = [1, 2, 3]` (length 3):
- i=0: sum = 0+1 = 1
- i=1: sum = 1+2 = 3
- i=2: sum = 3+3 = 6
- i=3: `xs[3]` is `undefined` (array has indices 0-2 only) → sum = 6 + undefined = `NaN`

Final: `NaN / 3 = NaN`, matching the observed `actual: NaN`. The "simplified" loop replaced a presumably correct `i < xs.length` with `i <= xs.length` — a classic off-by-one on the loop boundary, not a logic error in the sum/division itself (division by `xs.length` is correct once `sum` is correct).

## Call Chain
`avg([1,2,3])` → for-loop iterates 4 times instead of 3 → `sum` becomes `NaN` on the 4th iteration → returned value is `NaN` → `assert.equal(NaN, 2)` fails.

## Fix
```js
export function avg(xs) {
  let sum = 0
  for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++) sum += xs[i]
  return sum / xs.length
}
```
Single change: `i <= xs.length` → `i < xs.length`.

## Verification
Run `node --test test/avg.test.js` — `avg([1, 2, 3])` should return `2` and the assertion should pass. Additionally sanity-check an edge case mentally: `avg([])` → loop never runs, `sum = 0`, returns `0 / 0 = NaN` — that's expected/separate behavior (empty-array average is undefined), not part of this bug.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — hand-traced iteration count and index access directly reproduce `NaN` with the exact boundary (`<=`) present in the code; adversarial probe considered and ruled out: (1) wrong operator (`+=` vs something else)? No, `+=` is correct, the issue is only the operand becoming `undefined`. (2) `xs.length` itself wrong/mutated? No evidence, array literal is static and length is read consistently. (3) division bug? No — division is only `NaN` because the numerator is already `NaN`, not because of the denominator. No alternative explanation survives; the off-by-one in the loop bound is the sole and sufficient cause.

Fix: change to `i < xs.length`. Verify with `node --test test/avg.test.js` — expect pass with `avg([1,2,3]) === 2`.

## Critical

### `title()` will not compile under strict mode — `paging.ts:9` (the `title` function)
**Problem:** The parameter is typed `Item | null`, but `item.name.trim()` accesses `.name` with no null check or narrowing.
**Impact:** Under `strictNullChecks` (part of `strict: true`), this is a compile-time error (TS2531/2532: "Object is possibly 'null'") — the build fails, it never reaches runtime. If strict mode were somehow off, it would instead throw `Cannot read properties of null` for any caller that legitimately passes `null`, which the signature explicitly permits.
**Fix:** Guard the null case — either `if (item === null) return ''` (or whatever the no-item contract should be) before accessing `.name`, or narrow at the call site and drop `| null` from the signature if callers never actually pass null.

### Off-by-one in `pageOf()` returns 21 items, not 20 — `paging.ts:1-5`
**Problem:** `size` is fixed at 20, but `items.slice(start, start + size + 1)` requests a slice end of `start + 21`. `Array.prototype.slice`'s end index is exclusive, so the intended page size (20) only needs `start + size`.
**Impact:** Every page returns one extra item, and that item is the first item of the *next* page — pages overlap by one. Any caller treating `pageOf` as a clean partition of `items` (e.g., for rendering, counting, or re-combining pages) gets duplicated/wrong data. This is wrong-results-in-normal-operation, not an edge case.
**Fix:** `return items.slice(start, start + size)`.

### No bound on negative or out-of-range `page` — `paging.ts:4` (`start`)
**Problem:** `page` is untyped beyond `number` — no validation that it's a non-negative integer. If `page` is negative, `start = page * size` is negative, and `Array.prototype.slice` with a negative start index counts from the end of the array, silently returning unrelated items instead of failing or returning an empty page.
**Impact:** A caller bug (e.g., `page - 1` going negative on the first page) produces plausible-looking but wrong data instead of an error — this is the kind of defect that passes review and ships because nothing crashes.
**Fix:** Guard: `if (page < 0) throw new Error(...)` or clamp to 0, depending on the intended contract for `page`.

## Root Cause
`req.query.name` is concatenated directly into the SQL string instead of being passed as a parameterized value, so a name containing a single quote breaks out of the string literal and the leftover characters are parsed as SQL syntax.

## Evidence
The query is built as:
```js
"SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name = '" + req.query.name + "'"
```
Substituting `O'Brien` produces the literal string sent to Postgres:
```
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name = 'O'Brien'
```
Postgres's parser reads `'O'` as a complete, closed string literal, then encounters the bare token `Brien` where it expects an operator or end of clause — which is exactly the reported error, `syntax error at or near "Brien"`. The symptom report that "every other name works" is consistent with this: only names containing a character meaningful to SQL syntax (here, `'`) trigger a parse failure; this is the defining behavior of string concatenation into SQL, not of a parameterized query, which treats the entire value as opaque data regardless of its contents.

## Call Chain
`GET /customers?name=O'Brien` → route handler reads `req.query.name` unmodified → string-concatenated into the query → `db.query(...)` sends the malformed SQL to Postgres → Postgres parser rejects it → error propagates unhandled to a 500 response.

## Fix
Withheld — the root cause is a SQL injection vulnerability (unsanitized, unparameterized user input embedded directly into a SQL statement), which is out of scope for Pierce to patch. See handoff below. The patch itself must use a parameterized query (e.g. `db.query("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name = $1", [req.query.name])` or equivalent for the driver in use) rather than any form of manual escaping.

## Verification
After the parameterized fix is applied: `GET /customers?name=O'Brien` should return a normal JSON result (empty array or matching rows) instead of a 500, and `GET /customers?name='; DROP TABLE customers; --` should return an empty result set with the `customers` table still intact — confirming the apostrophe is treated as literal data, not as SQL syntax.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — Adversarial probe: considered whether this could be a driver-level encoding bug, a schema mismatch, or a transient Postgres issue instead of injection via concatenation. Ruled out: the error message names the exact substring (`Brien`) from the attacker-controlled input, which is only possible if that raw text was spliced into the SQL token stream — a parameterized query would never leak user input into a syntax-error position, since the value is never parsed as SQL regardless of its content. No alternative explanation produces an error message containing the literal tail of the input value. ## Root Cause
The `setInterval` callback is created exactly once (effect has an empty `[]` dependency array) and permanently closes over `count` from that first render — so every tick computes `setCount(0 + 1)` instead of reading the current state, pinning the counter at 1 forever.

## Evidence
- `useEffect(() => { ... }, [])` — empty deps means the effect body runs once, on mount, and is never re-run. The `id` returned by `setInterval` is created a single time with a single closure.
- Inside that closure, `setCount(count + 1)` references `count` via normal JS closure semantics — it reads whatever `count` was bound to at the time the closure was created, which is the initial render's value, `0`. React does not mutate closed-over variables when state updates; it only triggers a re-render with a *new* `count` binding in a *new* function call of `Ticker`, which this stale closure never sees.
- The console.log inside the interval firing every second rules out the interval itself being broken (confirms the symptom is isolated to the state update, not the timer) — this is exactly what you'd observe if the closure's `count` were frozen at 0: the interval fires every second, each time calling `setCount(1)`, and React bails out of re-rendering once the new value equals the current value after the first tick.

## Call Chain
`Ticker` mounts → effect runs once → `setInterval` closure captures `count=0` → tick 1: `setCount(0+1)` → state becomes 1, re-render happens (interval closure not recreated, still holds `count=0`) → tick 2: `setCount(0+1)` again → state already 1, React skips re-render → display stays at 1 indefinitely while the timer and its `console.log` keep firing.

## Fix
```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setCount(c => c + 1), 1000)
  return () => clearInterval(id)
}, [])
```
Using the functional updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` reads the latest state at update time instead of the value closed over at creation time, eliminating the stale closure without needing to add `count` to the dependency array (which would instead tear down/recreate the interval every second — a different, undesirable behavior).

## Verification
Apply the one-line change, reload `/dashboard`, and watch the `<span>` for 5+ seconds: it should read 1, 2, 3, 4, 5... incrementing every second instead of sticking at 1. Confirm no duplicate/leaked intervals by checking the console.log cadence stays at one log per second (not two), which also rules out a StrictMode double-invoke effect as a contributing factor.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — adversarial probe considered: (1) React 18 StrictMode double-invoking effects, which would produce two concurrent intervals and a count that either jumps by 2 per second or races — not consistent with a hard freeze at exactly 1; (2) batched state updates swallowing increments — doesn't explain a *permanent* freeze at 1 specifically, only occasional skipped renders. Neither alternative survives the exact observed symptom ("shows 1 forever," log firing every second), which only the stale-closure-via-empty-deps explanation accounts for precisely.

## Root Cause
The loop boundary uses `i <= xs.length` instead of `i < xs.length`, so on the last iteration `i` equals `xs.length` and `xs[xs.length]` is `undefined`; adding `undefined` to `sum` poisons it to `NaN`, which then propagates through the division.

## Evidence
Traced the arithmetic by hand against the exact input from the failing assertion, `avg([1, 2, 3])`:
- `xs.length` = 3, loop condition `i <= 3` → iterations run for `i = 0, 1, 2, 3` (four iterations, one too many)
- `i=0: sum = 0 + xs[0] = 1`
- `i=1: sum = 1 + xs[1] = 3`
- `i=2: sum = 3 + xs[2] = 6`
- `i=3: sum = 6 + xs[3]` → `xs[3]` is out of bounds → `undefined` → `6 + undefined = NaN`
- `return NaN / 3 = NaN`

This matches the observed actual value exactly (`NaN`), confirming the extra iteration — not the division, not the initial `sum = 0` — is what introduces the bad value.

## Call Chain
`avg(xs)` → loop runs one iteration past the last valid index → `sum` becomes `NaN` on that iteration → `sum / xs.length` returns `NaN` → test assertion `assert.equal(avg([1,2,3]), 2)` fails with actual `NaN`.

## Fix
Change the loop boundary from `<=` to `<`:

```js
export function avg(xs) {
  let sum = 0
  for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++) sum += xs[i]
  return sum / xs.length
}
```

Only the comparison operator changes. No other line is touched — no refactor of the loop into `reduce`/`for...of`, even though that would be tempting; that's cleanup, not the fix.

## Verification
Run `node --test test/avg.test.js` and confirm:
- `avg([1, 2, 3])` returns `2` (not `NaN`)
- the specific failing assertion `assert.equal(avg([1, 2, 3]), 2)` passes
- no new failures are introduced for edge cases already covered by the test file (e.g. empty array, single-element array) — worth a manual check since `avg([])` will still correctly return `NaN` (0/0), which is pre-existing behavior, not part of this bug.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — Evidence: manual trace of the exact failing input through the loop as written shows the fourth, out-of-bounds iteration is the sole point `NaN` enters. Adversarial probe: considered alternative causes — wrong `sum` initialization (ruled out, `0` is correct and never reassigned incorrectly before the OOB iteration), a type issue with the input array (ruled out, `[1,2,3]` are plain numbers), a division-by-zero on `xs.length` (ruled out, `length` is `3`, not `0`). ### Issue 1 — invoice total off by a cent

## Root Cause
`total` sums invoice amounts as native JS floating-point numbers, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact IEEE-754 double-precision binary representation, so their sum produces a representable-but-inexact result (`0.30000000000000004`) — an error class that was invisible before because amounts were stored as integer cents (exact integer addition), and became visible the moment the refactor switched the unit to float dollars.

## Evidence
- `total = items => items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)` — plain `+` on raw JS numbers, no rounding, no fixed-point/decimal library, no cents conversion.
- `0.1` and `0.2` in binary64 are themselves already rounded (`0.1` ≈ `0.1000000000000000055511151231257827...`), so their sum is guaranteed to drift from the mathematically exact `0.3` in general — this isn't a logic bug in `reduce`, it's a property of the representation being summed.
- The stated recent change ("totals moved from integer cents to float dollars") is the exact point where exact arithmetic (ints) was swapped for inexact arithmetic (floats) — consistent with the bug appearing now and not before.

## Call Chain
`test/invoice.test.js` calls `total([0.1, 0.2])` → `reduce` performs `0 + 0.1 + 0.2` in float64 → result is bit-for-bit `0.30000000000000004` → `assert.equal(result, 0.3)` fails because `0.3`'s float64 representation differs from the sum's representation.

## Fix
```js
export const total = items =>
  Math.round(items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) * 100) / 100
```
Minimal: round the final sum to cents precision after summing, so float noise beyond 2 decimal places is discarded. (Does not touch how individual line amounts are stored — only normalizes the aggregate.)

## Verification
Run `node --test test/invoice.test.js` — `assert.equal(total([0.1, 0.2]), 0.3)` must pass. Also spot-check a case that previously masked other drift, e.g. `total([1.01, 2.02, 3.03])` should equal `6.06` exactly after the patch (it would not, reliably, without the rounding step).

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — adversarial probe: considered "bug is in `assert.equal`'s precision handling" instead of `total`'s arithmetic — rejected, because `assert.equal` doing exact equality is correct/expected behavior for a test assertion; the inexactness originates in the value being compared, not the comparator. Considered "bug is in `reduce`'s initial value or iteration order" — rejected, reordering the inputs doesn't remove the representation error, it only changes which rounding bit flips. No alternative cause survives; the cause is float representation of 0.1/0.2, confirmed.

## Handoffs
→ ndv-build (implementation) · invoice total function (as given inline, no file path provided): confirmed root cause = float64 can't exactly represent 0.1/0.2, surfaced by the cents→dollars refactor. Fix: `Math.round(items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) * 100) / 100`. Verify via `node --test test/invoice.test.js` passing `assert.equal(total([0.1, 0.2]), 0.3)`.

→ ndv-architect (structure) · currency representation: storing/summing money as float dollars instead of integer cents (or a fixed-point/decimal type) is structurally unsound for currency — this test caught one instance, but every other summation, multiplication, or tax/discount calculation on these float amounts is equally exposed to the same drift. The rounding patch above fixes this call site, not the underlying representation choice.

## Root Cause
The original NaN came from an off-by-one loop bound (`i <= xs.length` instead of `i < xs.length`), which reads one slot past the end of the array; that out-of-bounds read returns `undefined`, and adding `undefined` into `sum` poisons the running total to `NaN`. The patch did not fix the boundary — it added `xs[i] || 0` to coerce the out-of-bounds `undefined` (and every other element) to a safe fallback value, so it's masking the symptom at the point of use, not correcting the loop that produces it.

## Evidence
Tracing the patched code by hand, not running it:
- `xs.length = n` → loop runs `i = 0..n` inclusive → `n + 1` iterations on an `n`-length array. The last iteration reads `xs[n]`, which is always `undefined` for any array, regardless of its contents.
- `undefined || 0` → `0`, so that extra iteration adds `0` to `sum`. For a non-empty array this happens to leave the sum numerically correct — not because the loop is right, but because the extra term is always zero.
- For `xs = []`: `xs.length = 0`, loop condition `i <= 0` still runs once (`i = 0`), reads `xs[0]` → `undefined` → `0`, so `sum = 0`. Return value is `0 / 0`, which is **still `NaN`** in JS.

That last line is the proof this isn't fixed: the exact symptom the ticket was opened for (`avg()` returning `NaN`) still reproduces on an empty-array input. The single passing test evidently doesn't call `avg([])`, so it can't see this.

## Call Chain
`avg(xs)` → off-by-one loop reads `xs[xs.length]` (out of bounds, `undefined`) → `|| 0` fallback hides the bad read for the sum, but doesn't touch the final `sum / xs.length` division → for `xs.length === 0` that division is `0/0` → `NaN` resurfaces unchanged.

## Fix
```diff
 export function avg(xs) {
+  if (xs.length === 0) return NaN // or 0, depending on intended semantics — needs a product decision
   let sum = 0
-  for (let i = 0; i <= xs.length; i++) sum += xs[i] || 0
+  for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++) sum += xs[i]
   return sum / xs.length
 }
```
Fixing the loop bound removes the out-of-bounds read entirely, so the `|| 0` guard is no longer needed (and shouldn't stay — it silently zeroes legitimate `0`/`NaN`/falsy numeric entries, which is a separate latent bug it introduces). Whether `avg([])` should throw, return `0`, or return `NaN` is a product decision the ticket doesn't settle — that gap is exactly why it wasn't caught.

## Verification
1. Add a test case: `assert.ok(Number.isNaN(avg([])) === <expected>)` once the empty-array behavior is decided, plus `avg([1,2,3]) === 2` and `avg([0,0,0]) === 0` to confirm the `|| 0` removal didn't change correct-case behavior.
2. Run `node --test test/avg.test.js` — all cases, including the new empty-array case, must pass with the loop-bound fix applied, not the `|| 0` patch.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** UNCONFIRMED for sign-off — root cause of the *mechanism* (off-by-one loop) is CONFIRMED by the hand-trace above, but the patch does not fix it, and an adversarial probe (`avg([])`) reproduces the original NaN symptom through the same unfixed boundary. One passing test cannot close a ticket whose own failure mode it never exercises. **Do not close the ticket.**

## Handoffs
→ ndv-build (implementation) · `avg()` function: replace `for (let i = 0; i <= xs.length; i++) sum += xs[i] || 0` with `for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i++) sum += xs[i]`; decide and implement the `xs.length === 0` return value explicitly. Verify via `node --test test/avg.test.js` after adding the test case below.
→ ndv-tester (coverage) · `test/avg.test.js`: current suite has exactly 1 passing test and does not cover `avg([])`, which still returns `NaN` under the current patch — add that case plus a case with a legitimate `0`-valued element to catch the `|| 0` masking bug.

## Triage

Class B — the message ("expected 1 users, got 2") names a wrong value, not a cause. Reading the one file given is enough to form and confirm a hypothesis; no deeper stack trace exists to chase.

## Root Cause

`creates a user` and `creates an admin` both act on the same module-level `db` singleton with no reset between them, and now that tests run in parallel, the runner no longer guarantees `creates a user` finishes before `creates an admin`'s `await createUser({ name: 'b', admin: true })` lands — so roughly 1 run in 20 the admin insert completes before the first test reads `db.users.all()`, and the count includes both tests' rows.

## Evidence

- `db` is imported once at module scope and explicitly commented as a singleton — both tests operate on the *same object instance*, not isolated fixtures.
- Neither test resets, clears, or scopes the db before/after running — there is no `beforeEach`/`afterEach` isolation visible.
- The only recent change cited is "tests now run in parallel." Node's module cache gives both tests the same singleton reference regardless of parallelism; what parallelism removes is the implicit sequencing that used to make test 1 always observe state before test 2 wrote anything.
- Failure rate (~1/20) is consistent with a narrow interleaving window — not with a deterministic logic bug (which would fail every run) and not with a flaky external dependency (nothing async/external is mentioned other than the shared db calls themselves).

**Adversarial probe:** could this instead be a bug in `db.users.all()`/`db.users.admins()` (e.g. one array backing both, off-by-one, double-insert on `createUser`)? If `all()` itself double-counted, the test would fail *every* run, not 1-in-20 — a logic bug doesn't care about scheduler timing. Could it be a retry/duplicate network call inside `createUser`? No evidence of network or retry logic in what's shown, and that would also produce a consistent, not intermittent, failure for a single test run in isolation. The only variable that changed and that correlates with intermittency is scheduling — which only matters if state is shared. No alternative explanation survives without also requiring shared mutable state, so the probe doesn't dislodge the hypothesis.

## Call Chain

`node --test` (parallel) → `creates an admin` test begins before/during `creates a user` → both call into the same `db` object → `creates a user`'s `db.users.all()` observes the admin's row too → assertion `equal(..., 1)` fails intermittently depending on interleaving.

## On "add `retry: 3` and move on" — **No.**

That's a symptom-side patch on a cause that's still live. Retrying doesn't fix the race, it just rolls the dice again on the same shared-state interleaving — with `retry: 3` the *visible* flake rate drops to roughly (1/20)^4, which will look like "fixed" in CI, but:
- the singleton still has no isolation, so any new test added to this file inherits the same race, at a flake rate that compounds with every additional test;
- it masks a real correctness signal: two tests silently sharing effects means a future test could pass only *because* another test's side effect happened to already be present — a false-positive bug, not just a false-negative flake;
- it's exactly the primordial-rule violation Pierce exists to catch — fixing the symptom instead of the shared mutable state.

## Verification (of the real fix, once applied)

Run `for i in $(seq 100); do node --test || break; done` after isolating state between tests (expect 0 failures, not a reduced failure rate). A fix that still fails at any rate under that loop is not a fix.

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — shared mutable singleton + newly-parallel scheduling is the only hypothesis consistent with both the intermittency and the specific off-by-one-user count; the probe for an alternative (a logic bug in `db.users`) fails because it would produce deterministic, not intermittent, failure.

## Handoffs

→ ndv-build (implementation) · `user.test.js` (both test bodies) / `src/db.js` (singleton export): Confirmed cause — shared `db` singleton with no per-test reset, exposed by parallel test execution. Fix — give each test an isolated db (either export a `createDb()` factory and construct a fresh instance per test file/test, or add a `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hook that clears all rows from the shared singleton before each test runs). Verify with the 100-iteration loop above showing zero failures.

→ ndv-architect (structure) · `src/db.js`: the db module exposes no reset/factory API, which is what forced tests onto a single shared singleton in the first place — worth a structural look at whether `db` should be constructible per-consumer rather than a module-level singleton, independent of the test-only fix above.

## Root Cause
`npm run worker` is being run with no `QUEUE_URL` set in the process environment — on a fresh clone there is no `.env` file (it's gitignored and never committed), and the recent provider migration renamed/replaced the old queue variable with `QUEUE_URL` in `.env.example`, so whatever `.env` does or doesn't exist locally was never updated to define it; `loadConfig`'s required-var check at `src/config.js:14` fails before `main` in `src/worker.js:3` can proceed.

## Evidence
- Error message is self-describing (Class A per triage): `Missing required environment variable QUEUE_URL` names the exact missing thing — no ambiguity requiring source inspection.
- Stack trace confirms the failure is a validation check, not a connection or runtime error: `loadConfig (src/config.js:14:11)` called directly from `main (src/worker.js:3:18)` — this is a startup guard firing, consistent with a config-presence check rather than a deeper bug.
- Stated context: "the queue moved to a new provider and `.env.example` was updated" — explains why the specific name is `QUEUE_URL` (new) rather than whatever the previous provider's variable was named, and why a fresh clone trips on it: the clone has no `.env` seeded with the new key.
- Reproduction is a bare `npm run worker` on a fresh clone — no prior setup step populated the environment, which is exactly the condition that triggers this guard.

## Call Chain
`main()` → `loadConfig()` reads `process.env.QUEUE_URL` → value is `undefined` → guard throws before any queue/network code runs. The failure is entirely at the config-validation boundary; nothing downstream (queue client, provider SDK) is reached yet.

## Fix
No source change. Ensure the environment `npm run worker` runs in defines `QUEUE_URL`:
- Copy `.env.example` → `.env` if `.env` doesn't exist yet, or add the `QUEUE_URL` line to an existing `.env`.
- Set its value to the real connection string/endpoint for the new queue provider (not the placeholder from `.env.example`).

`src/config.js` is doing its job correctly here — it's catching a genuinely missing required value, not misbehaving.

## Verification
1. Confirm the gap: `grep -q '^QUEUE_URL=' .env 2>/dev/null && echo present || echo absent` — expect `absent` before the fix.
2. Apply the fix (add/update `QUEUE_URL=<real-value>` in `.env`).
3. Re-run `npm run worker` — it should pass `loadConfig` without throwing and proceed into the worker's normal startup (next observable behavior: connecting to the queue, not a config error).
4. If it still throws the same error, the loader isn't reading `.env` at all (e.g., no `dotenv` require/import in the entrypoint) — that's a distinct root cause and should be reopened as its own investigation, not patched as a guess here.

## Verdict
**CONFIRMED.** Adversarial probe: the two plausible alternative explanations for this exact message — (a) `.env` truly absent on the fresh clone, vs. (b) a `.env` exists but wasn't updated with the renamed key — both collapse to the identical required action (ensure `QUEUE_URL` is defined in the environment used at runtime), so neither alternative survives as a *different* fix to pursue. A third alternative (dotenv not loaded at all) is distinguishable only by step 4 of Verification and is explicitly flagged there as a separate investigation if it occurs, not silently absorbed into this fix.

## Handoffs (if any)
None. No security, performance, architectural, or coverage concerns surfaced — this is a straightforward Class A config gap with a self-describing error, and the error already gave a clear, loud signal, so no `ndv-telemetry` gap either.

**Completeness check** — symptom (timeout for Platform/4,000 members, sub-second for small teams), reproduction (`GET /teams/42/members`), location (production, this endpoint), recent change (avatar lookups added last week) are all present and specific. Pass.

## Root Cause
The handler fetches each member's avatar with a separate `await`ed query inside a `for` loop — an N+1 query pattern with zero batching or parallelism — so total handler latency scales linearly with team size, and at 4,000 members the accumulated round-trip time exceeds the 30s timeout.

## Evidence
Reading the handler directly (full source given, no further files needed):

```js
for (const m of members) {
  m.avatar = await db.query('SELECT url FROM avatars WHERE member_id = $1', [m.id])
}
```

- One `await` per member, executed **serially** — no `Promise.all`, no `WHERE member_id = ANY($1)` / `IN (...)`, no `JOIN` against `avatars`.
- Total latency ≈ `N × L` where `L` is one round-trip's cost. For N=4000, even a modest per-query cost (single-digit-to-low-double-digit ms, realistic for pool-contended sequential round trips) pushes total time well past 30s. For small teams (N small), `N × L` stays under a second — matching the observed split exactly.
- The timing correlates with **member count**, not with the size of the `members` table scan — the one-shot `SELECT * FROM members WHERE team_id = $1` runs for every team regardless of size and isn't itself a plausible source of a count-scaled timeout, since small teams hit the same query path and return in under a second.
- Matches "changed recently: avatars added last week" — before that, there was no per-row loop, so no mechanism existed for latency to scale with member count.

**Adversarial probe (for CONFIRMED verdict):** checked for alternative explanations —
- *Missing index on `members.team_id`* — would scale with table size, not with the specific team's member count in a way that explains a sharp per-team split; and it wouldn't explain why small teams return in under a second from the same table.
- *Connection-pool exhaustion* — plausible as a compounding factor at N=4000 serialized acquisitions, but it is a consequence of the same serial-loop pattern, not an independent cause; removing the loop removes this too.
- *Avatars table itself slow/missing index on `member_id`* — would add constant-per-call overhead but still requires the N+1 loop structure to turn that constant cost into a 4000x multiplier. The loop structure is the determining factor, not a per-query index issue.

No alternative root cause survives the probe.

## Call Chain
`GET /teams/42/members` → one `members` query (fast) → loop of 4,000 sequential `avatars` queries, each awaited before the next starts → cumulative latency exceeds the 30s request timeout → client sees a timeout, not an error from the DB.

## Verdict
**CONFIRMED** — the N+1, serially-awaited avatar lookup is the cause; evidence is the loop structure itself (no batching/parallelism) combined with the exact symptom shape (latency scales with member count, introduced at the same time the avatar feature was added), and no alternative cause survives the adversarial probe.

## Handoffs
This root cause is a performance bottleneck, not a logic bug — out of scope for me to fix.

**Handoff → ndv-optimize (performance):** `GET /teams/:id/members` handler — N+1 query pattern, one serially-awaited `avatars` query per member instead of a single batched fetch (e.g. `WHERE member_id = ANY($1)` or a `JOIN`), causing handler latency to scale linearly with team size; confirmed as the cause of the 30s timeout for the 4,000-member 'Platform' team.

The off-by-one (`i <= xs.length`) is still there; the patch just coerces the resulting `undefined` read (`xs[xs.length]`) to `0` with `|| 0` so it stops poisoning the sum with `NaN`. That's a guard on the *symptom* (NaN appearing in sum), not a fix of the *cause* (loop reads one index past the array).

## Evidence

Now `undefined || 0` → `0`, so that extra iteration becomes a no-op addition. The bug that *caused* NaN is still present; it's just defanged for this input shape.

## Root Cause
JavaScript's `Number` type is IEEE‑754 double-precision, which cannot represent most decimal fractions (including 0.1 and 0.2) exactly — so `0.1 + 0.2` evaluates to the nearest representable double, `0.30000000000000004`, not `0.3`. This is a deterministic property of binary floating point, not a bug in `reduce` or the comparison.

## Evidence
- The function given: `total = items => items.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)` — plain float addition, no rounding anywhere in the chain.
- `0.1` and `0.2` each round to the nearest representable binary64 value when parsed; neither is exact. Adding those two approximations produces `0.30000000000000004`, which is a different double than the one `0.3` parses to — hence `assert.equal` (which for numbers is strict equality) fails.
- Confirmed by the stated recent change: totals moved from integer cents (exact integer arithmetic, no representation error possible) to float dollars (inexact for most 2-decimal values). That migration is the proximate cause of the regression — the bug didn't exist under the integer-cents representation because integers have no fractional representation error.

## Call Chain
`total([0.1, 0.2])` → `reduce` accumulates `0 + 0.1 = 0.1` → `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004` → returned value compared against literal `0.3` → mismatch → assertion failure.

## Fix
Do the summation in integer cents internally, converting back to dollars once at the end — this is the same trick the old integer-cents code relied on, just scoped to the function instead of the whole data model:

```js
export const total = items =>
  items.reduce((s, x) => s + Math.round(x * 100), 0) / 100
```

Rounding to cents *before* summing (rather than rounding the running float sum after each addition) avoids re-introducing drift across many items.

## Verification
Run `node --test test/invoice.test.js`. `assert.equal(total([0.1, 0.2]), 0.3)` should now pass because `Math.round(0.1*100) + Math.round(0.2*100) = 10 + 20 = 30`, and `30 / 100` produces the same double that the literal `0.3` parses to. Also worth re-running any other cases in that test file with more line items (e.g. 3+ values) to confirm no drift reappears — if the suite only has this one assertion, that's a gap worth flagging (see handoff below).

## Verdict
**Verdict:** CONFIRMED. The only mechanism that produces exactly `0.30000000000000004` from `0.1 + 0.2` in JS is IEEE‑754 double rounding. No alternative cause survives.

Off-by-one loop boundary: `i <= xs.length` lets the loop run one iteration past the last valid index, so it reads `xs[xs.length]` — out of bounds, `undefined` — and adds it into `sum`, poisoning the accumulator to `NaN`.

- `i=2`: `sum = 3 + 3 = 6`
- `i=3` (should not execute — `xs[3]` doesn't exist): `sum = 6 + undefined = NaN`
